```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r}
library(z3r)
ctx <- z3_context()
```

Every Z3 expression has a *sort*: its type. z3r keeps sorts strict and
numbers exact. This vignette explains how R values become Z3 values, what
each operator means for each sort, and how results come back to R.

## Sorts

```{r}
z3_int_sort(ctx)
z3_real_sort(ctx)
z3_bool_sort(ctx)
z3_bv_sort(ctx, 16)
z3_string_sort(ctx)
z3_array_sort(z3_int_sort(ctx), z3_bool_sort(ctx))
z3_uninterpreted_sort(ctx, "Person")
```

`Int` is the mathematical integers, with no overflow. `Real` is the exact
reals: rationals, and algebraic numbers such as the square root of 2 in
models. Neither is a machine type. Fixed-width machine integers are
bit-vectors (see `vignette("bitvectors")`) and IEEE doubles are the floating
point sorts (see `vignette("floating-point")`).

Constants are created with a name and a sort. The same name and sort give
the same constant:

```{r}
x <- z3_int(ctx, "x")
z3_identical(x, z3_int(ctx, "x"))
v <- z3_reals(ctx, c("a", "b", "c"))
z3_sort(v$a)
z3_sort_kind(v$a)
```

## From R values to Z3 values

`z3_int_val()` and `z3_real_val()` build exact numerals. Strings are the
safe way to give large or fractional values:

```{r}
z3_int_val(ctx, "123456789012345678901234567890")
z3_real_val(ctx, "1/3")
z3_real_val(ctx, "0.125")
z3_real_val(ctx, "-2.5e-3")
```

Z3's own numeral parser silently misreads some malformed strings, so z3r
validates them first:

```{r, error = TRUE}
z3_real_val(ctx, "1/-3")
z3_real_val(ctx, "1.2.3")
```

R numbers mixed with expressions are converted by a fixed rule:

* whole numbers become exact integers;
* whole numbers beyond 2^53 are refused, because R may already have
  rounded them;
* other doubles become the rational of their shortest decimal form, so
  `0.1` is 1/10, the value R prints;
* `NA`, `NaN` and `Inf` are refused.

```{r, error = TRUE}
r <- z3_real(ctx, "r")
r + 0.1
x + 2^53
x + 2^60
```

`options(z3r.doubles = "error")` makes every non-integer double an error,
which forces exact strings everywhere. `gmp` numbers convert exactly:

```{r}
x * gmp::as.bigz("100000000000000000000")
r + gmp::as.bigq(1, 7)
```

## Operators

| Operator | Int / Real | Bool | bit-vector | floating point |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+ - *` | arithmetic | error | modular | IEEE, round to nearest even |
| `/` | exact real division | error | error | IEEE division |
| `^` | power | error | error | error |
| `%/% %%` | Int: SMT-LIB div, mod | error | error | `%%`: IEEE remainder |
| `== !=` | equation | equivalence | equation | structural equality |
| `< <= > >=` | comparison | error | error | IEEE comparison |
| `& \| !` | error | logic | bitwise | error |

Int and Real mix by promoting the Int exactly. Everything else must have
matching sorts:

```{r, error = TRUE}
p <- z3_bool(ctx, "p")
x + r
x + p
```

Z3's C API would have accepted `x + p` by converting the Boolean to 0 or 1;
z3r refuses, because that is almost always a mistake.

### Division

`/` is real division, as in R:

```{r}
x / 2
z3_sort_kind(x / 2)
```

`%/%` and `%%` are integer division and modulus with the SMT-LIB
(Euclidean) convention: the remainder is never negative. This agrees with R
for positive divisors and differs for negative ones:

```{r}
i <- function(v) z3_int_val(ctx, v)
c(z3 = z3_value(z3_simplify(i(-7) %/% 2)), R = -7 %/% 2)
c(z3 = z3_value(z3_simplify(i(7) %/% -2)), R = 7 %/% -2)
c(z3 = z3_value(z3_simplify(i(7) %% -2)), R = 7 %% -2)
```

`z3_rem()` has the sign of the divisor. Division by zero is not an error in
SMT: `x / 0` is some unspecified value, the same each time.

### Powers

A literal whole exponent up to 64 is expanded into a product, so the result
keeps the sort of the base. Other powers use Z3's real power operator:

```{r}
x^3
z3_sort_kind(x^3)
z3_sort_kind(x^x)
```

### Scalars only

z3r expressions are single formulas. R's recycling would silently build
the wrong formula, so vectors are refused:

```{r, error = TRUE}
x + 1:3
```

Build several constraints with `lapply()` or `Map()` instead.

### No accidental logic

A formula never turns into `TRUE` or `FALSE`:

```{r, error = TRUE}
if (x > 0) "positive"
```

## From Z3 values back to R

`z3_value()` returns a double only when the value is exactly representable;
otherwise a `gmp` number, or the exact string when gmp is missing:

```{r}
z3_value(z3_int_val(ctx, 42))
z3_value(z3_real_val(ctx, "1/4"))
z3_value(z3_real_val(ctx, "1/3"))
z3_value(z3_int_val(ctx, "9007199254740993"))
z3_value(z3_real_val(ctx, "1/3"), exact = FALSE)
```

Irrational algebraic numbers come from nonlinear real problems. They have no
exact R value, so `z3_value()` asks for `exact = FALSE`:

```{r, error = TRUE}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, r^3 == 2)
z3_check(s)
cube_root <- z3_eval(z3_model(s), r)
cube_root
z3_value(cube_root)
z3_value(cube_root, exact = FALSE)
z3_decimal(cube_root, 30)
```

`vignette("algebraic")` shows exact arithmetic on such numbers.

## Simplification and printing

```{r}
z3_simplify(x + 2 * x - 3 + 3)
z3_simplify((x + 1)^2, som = TRUE)
head(z3_simplify_help(ctx)[, c("name", "kind")])
```

Expressions print in SMT-LIB2 prefix form. `z3_set_print_mode()` switches a
context to Z3's low-level form, which shows shared subterms.
